lead: The Raimondi and Boyd charts turn two numbers — the Sommerfeld number S and the length-to-diameter ratio L/D — into everything else a journal bearing needs: how far off centre the shaft sits, the thinnest oil film, the friction torque, the oil flow and the temperature rise. They exist because the oil-film pressure in a bearing of finite length has no closed-form solution; it was solved numerically once and published as curves. A designer with a chart and five minutes can size a bearing for a pump, a gearbox or a turbine.
prereq: You need: the Sommerfeld number from Chapter 5.4 and the minimum film thickness idea from Chapter 5.3.

blocks.text: Oil in a loaded journal bearing is dragged through a gap that narrows in the direction of rotation. The Reynolds equation gives the pressure in that film. In a bearing of finite length, oil also escapes sideways at the two ends, so the pressure drops near each end — and that end effect kills any clean formula. Raimondi and Boyd solved the equation numerically over a wide range of running conditions and published the answers as families of curves. Every curve in a chart is one value of L/D; every point on a curve is one Sommerfeld number S.

The Sommerfeld number is S = (r/c)² (μ n / P). Here μ is the oil viscosity in Pa·s, n the shaft speed in rev/s, r the journal radius, c the radial clearance and P = W/(L d) the unit bearing pressure in Pa, with W the load, L the bearing length and d the journal diameter.
You supply the two inputs and read the outputs below.

head: Chart gives
What it tells you
Symbol

fraction of flow lost at the ends

blocks.text: The curves assume a full 360° bearing, steady load, a Newtonian oil, no misalignment, no oil groove inside the load-carrying arc and no turbulence. Break one of these and the chart value is a good first guess, not the truth.

items: Fix L/D between 0.5 and 1.5. Long bearings (L/D above 1) carry more load but run hotter and hate misalignment; short bearings leak more oil. L/D = 1 is a common first choice.
Compute S = (r/c)² (μ n / P) as in Chapter 5.4, using the oil viscosity at the temperature you expect in the film, not in the supply tank.
On the eccentricity chart, take the curve for your L/D and read ε at your S. Between two printed curves, interpolate in proportion.
Convert to the thinnest film: h_min = c(1 − ε), where c is the radial clearance, half the diametral clearance C. Compare h_min with the surface finish and with shaft misalignment.
On the friction chart, at the same S and the same L/D curve, read the friction variable (r/c)f. The friction coefficient is f = (r/c)f ÷ (r/c).
Torque T = f W r, with W the load in N and r the journal radius in m. Power lost as heat P_loss = T ω = 2π n T, with n in rev/s.
Read the flow variable to get the oil flow: Q = [Q/(r c n L)] × r c n L, where Q is in m³/s, r and c in m, L in m and n in rev/s. That sizes the supply pump and the drain.
Read the temperature-rise chart for ΔT.

blocks.text: h_min = c(1 − ε)     f = [(r/c)f] / (r/c)     T = f W r     P_loss = 2π n T
blocks.where: c is the radial clearance (m), ε the eccentricity ratio, (r/c)f the friction variable read from the chart, r the journal radius (m), W the load (N), n the shaft speed (rev/s), T the friction torque (N·m) and P_loss the power turned into heat (W).

sections.h3: The temperature loop and the limits

blocks.text: The charts were drawn for a fixed viscosity, yet the oil that carries the load also gets hot, and hot oil is thinner. So the last chart feeds back into the first. Take the inlet oil temperature, add the chart's ΔT to get the outlet temperature, average the two for the mean film temperature, look up the viscosity there and recompute S. Then read the charts once more. Two passes usually settle it; a third moves the answer very little. Only a few universities ask for the full loop in an exam — run it as a check that the first answer is not badly off.

Two limits. Bearing metal runs hotter than the oil leaving the bearing, so never quote the oil outlet temperature as the bearing temperature. And the charts lose accuracy at very high eccentricity, around ε above 0.95, where the film is thinner than the surface roughness, and in turbulent or heavily grooved bearings.

examples.question: A 50 mm diameter journal bearing carries a steady load W = 10 kN at n = 25 rev/s. The radial clearance is c = 0.05 mm and L/D = 1. The Sommerfeld number is S = 0.031. From the Raimondi and Boyd charts at S = 0.031 and L/D = 1, read ε = 0.62 and (r/c)f = 1.9. Find the minimum film thickness, the coefficient of friction, the friction torque and the power lost.
steps: Journal radius r = d/2 = 50/2 = 25 mm = 0.025 m. Radial clearance c = 0.05 mm.
Minimum film thickness: h_min = c(1 − ε) = 0.05 × (1 − 0.62) = 0.05 × 0.38 = 0.019 mm = 19 μm.
Friction torque: T = f W r = 0.0038 × 10 000 × 0.025 = 0.95 N·m.
Power lost as heat: P_loss = T ω = 0.95 × 157.08 = 149.23 W, about 0.15 kW.
Check: 19 μm of film is comfortable against the roughness of a ground journal, so the design is acceptable; the next step is to confirm the oil can carry 149 W away.
examples.answer: h_min = 0.019 mm (19 μm), f = 0.0038, T = 0.95 N·m and the power lost is 149.23 W (about 0.15 kW).
examples.check:
import math
c = 0.05        # radial clearance, mm
r = 25.0        # journal radius, mm
W = 10000.0     # load, N
n = 25.0        # speed, rev/s
eps = 0.62
rcf = 1.9
h_min = c * (1 - eps)
f = rcf / (r / c)
T = f * W * (r / 1000.0)
omega = 2 * math.pi * n
P = T * omega
print(round(h_min, 3))
print(round(f, 4))
print(round(T, 2))
print(round(omega, 2))
print(round(P, 2))

traps: S is dimensionless: put n in rev/s and viscosity in Pa·s. Feed rpm into S and every chart reading is wrong.
(r/c)f is not f. The chart gives the friction variable; divide by r/c (500 in the example) to get f = 0.0038.
Read the curve for your own L/D. The same S on the L/D = 0.5 curve gives a different ε than on the L/D = 1 curve.
h_min uses the radial clearance c, half the diametral clearance C. Using C doubles the film thickness you report.
Use viscosity at the working film temperature, not at the supply temperature; the chart answer is optimistic otherwise.

quiz.q: What two quantities do you need before opening the Raimondi and Boyd charts?
quiz.a: The Sommerfeld number S and the length-to-diameter ratio L/D.

quiz.q: Write the formula for minimum film thickness.
quiz.a: h_min = c(1 − ε), where c is the radial clearance and ε the eccentricity ratio.

quiz.q: Why is there a separate curve for each L/D?
quiz.a: Side leakage at the two ends depends on bearing length. Two bearings with the same S but different L/D have different pressure fields, so ε, friction and flow all differ.

quiz.q: A chart gives (r/c)f = 2.0. Why is the friction coefficient not 2.0?
quiz.a: The ordinate is the friction coefficient multiplied by the clearance ratio r/c, which is large. f = 2.0/(r/c); for r/c = 400, f = 0.005.

quiz.q: At S = 0.15 and L/D = 1 the chart gives ε ≈ 0.45. The radial clearance is 0.04 mm. Find h_min and the film thickness ratio.
A bearing has W = 15 kN, r = 30 mm, n = 20 rev/s and friction coefficient f = 0.004. Find the power lost.
The charts give ε = 0.95 for a proposed bearing. What is the risk, and what can you change?
quiz.a: The film is only 5% of clearance, close to the surface roughness and misalignment, so metallic contact is possible. Raise S with a more viscous oil or a larger L/D (more projected area, lower pressure), improve cooling and alignment. Shrinking the clearance raises S but also shrinks h_min directly, so recheck h_min.

quiz.q: Two students read different ε from the same S. Give two likely reasons.
quiz.a: They used different L/D curves; or one put speed in rpm instead of rev/s; or they took viscosity at different oil temperatures.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern bearing design solves the Reynolds equation numerically for the actual groove and misalignment pattern, and adds the energy equation so viscosity varies across the film — thermo-hydrodynamic analysis. The printed charts survive as a quick sanity check and as a way to see trends. Digitised versions of these curves are common in open teaching material. Search 'finite journal bearing Reynolds equation', 'thermohydrodynamic lubrication' and 'bearing design charts digitised'.
